Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee

Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.
Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.
Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.
These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.
In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.
A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.
This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.

articles.title: Goodbye, SPNEC: MVP rebrands Leviste’s solar firm, lines up P5-B deal
articles.summary: A new name, five more solar businesses, and a possible "re-IPO," but Meralco's makeover can't quite banish Leviste's past or the P10.34-billion headache that comes with it

blocks.text: A new name, five more solar businesses, and a possible "re-IPO," but Meralco's makeover can't quite banish Leviste's past or the P10.34-billion headache that comes with it

items: Manuel V. Pangilinan is rebranding SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) to MGEN Renewables Inc. (MGENR) and integrating nearly P5 billion worth of renewable energy businesses.

The rebranding is part of a broader strategy by the Meralco group, distancing from the controversial past of Leandro Leviste's Solar Philippines, which faced contract terminations and financial obligations.
MGEN Renewables plans to strengthen its position by acquiring stakes in five solar businesses and is considering a 're-IPO' in March 2027, with expectations of improved financial performance.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Manuel V. Pangilinan is giving Leandro Leviste’s old solar crown jewel quite the makeover. First, shed the SPNEC name. Next, bring in nearly P5 billion worth of other renewable energy businesses.
And perhaps, pitch the shiny new thing to stock market investors all over again.

SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) is now officially MGEN Renewables Inc., (MGENR) after securing Securities and Exchange Commission approval on Monday, October 26; its stock ticker is also set to change to MGENR.

Officially, the renaming is part of the Meralco group’s broader rebranding strategy. Conveniently, it also removes a reminder of Solar Philippines, the controversial empire Leviste built before Pangilinan’s group took control.
And there’s quite a history behind SPNEC.

blocks.caption: FROM SPNEC to MGENR. This Rappler diagram shows the ownership of the rebranded solar company as of September 1, 2026 and before the proposed share swap. Diagram by Raphael Reyes/Rappler.

blocks.text: Leviste made his fortune assembling landholdings and securing solar development rights that attracted deep-pocketed investors, including Pangilinan himself. Industry sources that Rappler spoke with describe the young billionaire as a talented “flipper.”
But getting the rights to build solar farms and actually getting them built are two different businesses.

The Department of Energy (DOE) terminated 33 contracts tied to Leviste’s wider Solar Philippines group, covering around 11,400 megawatts of proposed capacity, and sought around P24 billion in financial obligations. His camp disputes the claims.
While much of the P24-billion mess relates to Leviste’s other companies, SPNEC is dragged into this too.
In a December 23, 2025 letter seen by Rappler, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin terminated the service contract for SPNEC’s 280-megawatt Santa Rosa Nueva Ecija 2 project and demanded P10.34 billion.

The DOE cited missed work-program commitments, an unrenewed performance bond, and missing documents, including a feasibility study and proof of land rights. Most of the demand came from P12.38 billion in work-program commitments, less P2.04 billion credited for reported accomplishments.

MGEN insists SPNEC is legally separate from Solar Philippines and not liable for the wider group’s P24 billion obligation. But it acknowledges that Santa Rosa belongs to SPNEC and says that it invoked force majeure over transmission delays and sought reconsideration.
Separately, Leviste and his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, face graft and plunder complaints involving solar contracts awarded to Leviste-linked companies. Both deny wrongdoing.

Leviste himself has kept his distance from his now Meralco-controlled company, resigning from the board in January and cashing out P3-billion worth of shares, leaving his holding company with an 11.51% stake.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] As Leandro Leviste cashes out of SPNEC, his private companies remain at the table

blocks.text: So, what’s next for MGENR?

On Tuesday, October 27, MGEN Renewables’ board approved a proposed P4.98-billion deal to take in stakes in five solar businesses from its controlling shareholder, MGEN Renewable Energy Inc., another Meralco subsidiary.
The companies have interests in operating solar plants across Luzon:

items: Greenergy for Global Inc. – 52.7-megawatt solar plant in Isabela
Greentech Solar Energy Inc. – 19.8-megawatt solar plant in Nueva Ecija
CACI Power Corporation – Linked to an 80.1-megawatt solar plant in Rizal
Nuevo Solar Energy Corporation – 68.7-megawatt solar plant in Ilocos Norte
PowerSource First Bulacan Solar Inc. – 55-megawatt solar plant in Bulacan

blocks.text: Instead of paying cash, MGEN Renewables will issue around 3.1 billion new shares to its controlling shareholder. If completed, the share swap deal would strengthen Meralco’s control while further diluting Leviste and other investors.
Then comes the more intriguing possibility, a “re-IPO” targeted for March 2027.
Since Leviste already took SPNEC public in 2021, this would be another share offering in the now bigger company under Meralco’s control, rather than a second listing. Nothing has been finalized.

This time, there’s more to show investors. Its P200-billion MTerra Solar project began commercial operations in August, while MGEN Renewables forecasts P774 million in profit for 2026, reversing a P4.1-billion loss in 2025.
The group also plans to invest up to another P7.815 billion in Terra Solar, subject to lender and investor approvals. – Rappler.com

articles.title: John Healey to end standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes
articles.summary: As budget looms, chancellor says he will ask Ofgem to remove ‘unfair and outdated’ fixed daily fee in 2027 or soon after

blocks.text: John Healey is abolishing standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes in a move he says will end an “unfair and outdated” practice and save two-thirds of households an average of £45 a year.

Ahead of his first budget statement in the Commons later on Wednesday, the chancellor said he would ask Ofgem, the energy regulator for Great Britain, to remove these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household – next year or as soon as possible after.
A standing charge is a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill, regardless of usage. A household could use no gas at all but still must pay the standing charge.
The Treasury said the move could save 60% of account-holding households an average of £45 off their annual bill.

Andy Burnham said: “Abolishing gas standing charges is about basic fairness and giving people more control over their bills. I am determined to reform our broken energy market, so it better serves the public interest.”
The prime minister has talked of reforming a “broken” energy market to serve households better, and said a week ago that he was asking the Treasury to look into the issue.
Healey said: “Gas standing charges are unfair and outdated so I am scrapping them to give millions of households a bit of breathing space.

“My budget will draw a line in the sand on an energy policy that has failed British billpayers for years, letting extra costs on bills pile high and leaving households even more exposed to global shocks.”
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, added that she would “keep doing everything I can to protect people from unaffordable bills”.

Greg Jackson, the founder and chief executive of Octopus Energy Group, welcomed the move, saying: “This represents real joined-up thinking to make a fairer, more efficient energy system, delivering what customers want – lower standing charges and further improving the ratio of electricity to gas prices.
“Most customers would see a cut in their gas bills, which is crucial, but would also enjoy even higher savings if they can move to heat pumps when it suits them.”
after newsletter promotion
This follows the government’s VAT cut on electricity bills that came into effect at the beginning of this month.

It means the energy price cap, set by Ofgem, from October was £45 a year less than it would have been. About a third of households on fixed tariffs are not affected by the price cap, meaning their electricity prices will have fallen when the VAT cut took effect.
More controversially, the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea but also announced a new energy wealth fund to support investment in cheap, clean power.

articles.title: Palace: P50-million bounty on Bato dela Rosa shows use of confidential funds
articles.summary: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro justified the interior department's P50 million bounty on at-large Sen. Bato dela Rosa, saying confidential funds should be used on such operations.

blocks.text: October 28, 2026 | 3:23pm

DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla and PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. hold a press briefing at Camp Crame to announce a P50- million reward for the arrest of Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, whom they consider ‘armed and dangerous.’
The Philippine STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Palace on Tuesday, October 27, again defended the P50-million bounty for information that will lead to the arrest of Sen. Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, clarifying that the money will come from the interior department's intelligence and confidential funds, not from the president.

"Ito ang mga operasyon na dapat na pinaglalaanan talaga ng pondo. Pero kung ito ay istratehiya nila, para mas mapabilis ang paghuli kay Sen. Bato, hindi ibig sabihin na dapat pang manggaling kay Pangulo na magsabi na 'ito ang dapat ninyong ibigay na bounty’ dahil ang DILG (Department of Interior and Local Government) at PNP (Philippine National Police) ay mayroong sariling mandato at mayroon po silang sariling pondo," she said.

(These are the operations that should be funded. But if this is their strategy to speed up Sen. Bato's capture, the president does not need to dictate the size of the bounty because the DILG and PNP have their own mandates and funding.)
The bounty was announced on October 23 during a press briefing by Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, where Dela Rosa was declared "armed and dangerous."
Remulla also gave Dela Rosa a week-long deadline to surrender, which will lapse on Thursday, October 29.
According to Castro, the deadline was given to allow the fugitive senator to surrender "properly and without needing police intervention."
"But if a person asked to surrender is stubborn and seems to be taking advantage of the government and law enforcement, they will be hunted down," she added.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant of arrest for Dela Rosa in November 2025 in connection with charges of crimes against humanity linked to the Duterte administration’s war on drugs. Dela Rosa, now the most wanted fugitive in the country, led the national police force during the initial and most intensive phase of the anti-drug crackdown.

Former president Rodrigo Duterte was charged with crimes against humanity of murder and is currently detained at the ICC Detention Center at The Hague in the Netherlands. The opening of Duterte's trial is scheduled for Nov. 30, 2026.

articles.summary: Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brings #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during the public forum to define what a liveable city should be

blocks.text: Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brings #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during the public forum to define what a liveable city should be

items: Rappler's MovePH hosted the #MoveCebu forum at the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 participants to discuss what makes a city livable.
Memoranda of Understanding were signed with the University of San Carlos and the University of the Philippines Cebu to enhance campus journalism and civic engagement.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Last week, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brought #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during a public forum to define what a liveable city should be.

To solidify our long-term commitment to campus journalism and civic engagement, we proudly signed memoranda of understanding with the University of San Carlos, and the University of the Philippines Cebu.

Rappler multimedia reporter John Sitchon, who reports on Cebu and the Visayas region, joined us as we worked directly with participants. You can check out these stories to read more about what happened during the roadshow:

items: Padayon Cebu: A new space to chat how to make the province more livable
At #MoveCebu forum, Cebuanos define what a liveable city should be
MovePH trains Movers in Cebu on local reporting, civic organizing

blocks.text: Taking advantage of the momentum generated by the forum, we dove into focused workshops with 35 newly-trained Movers, and leaders from Cebu’s civil society groups to bridge reporting with civic organizing.
Our Movers who chose the civic mobilization track pitched bold, ground-level initiatives tackling community realities across Cebu province.

For example, participants designed action plans to address food safety at the Colon Night Market. Some Movers want to address the lack of housing for displaced families in Minglanilla. One Mover hoped to champion the rights of people with dwarfism.

Meanwhile, Movers who wanted to specialize in community journalism pitched stories tackling gut issues in Cebu, like substandard flood control projects, child labor, and how neighborhood carinderias navigate inflation to keep meals affordable.

Our civil society and academe partners matched this energy during our Partners’ Huddle, where they decided to prioritize four crisis clusters: Ecological, Governance, Services, and Displacement. Together, partners committed to lobbying local councils to prioritize environmental policy over profit, conducting citizen audits, raising awareness of and tackling the energy crisis plaguing Cebu, and fighting for humane relocation sites and protected municipal waters for fishing communities.

Movers and partners are already coordinating on next steps in the Padayon Cebu chat room on the Muni app. To be part of the action, you can join the chat room by downloading the Rappler app for free. If you would like to support Rappler’s Cebu coverage, we hope you consider becoming a Rappler+ member. Rappler+ is our premium membership program that allows you to experience the best of our journalism, while supporting our work. You can join Rappler+ here. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Over 141,000 personnel to be deployed for Undas 2026
articles.summary: More than 141,000 personnel from the Philippine National Police (PNP) and partner agencies will be deployed nationwide for security and public safety operations during Undas 2026.

blocks.text: More than 141,000 personnel from the Philippine National Police (PNP) and partner agencies will be deployed nationwide for security and public safety operations during Undas 2026.

“A grand total of 141,172. This comprises our PNP personnel, other units, yung mga partner agencies natin, like [Armed Forces of the Philippines], [Bureau of Fire Protections], [Philippuine Coast Guard], and of course, yung force multipliers po natin mga tanod and other [non-government organizations]," PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said at a press briefing.

(A grand total of 141,172. This comprises our PNP personnel, other units, our partner agencies, like Armed Forces of the Philippines, Bureau of Fire Protections, Philippine Coast Guard, and of course, our force multipliers.)

The deployment aims to help ensure public safety and maintain peace and order as Filipinos travel to their home provinces and visit cemeteries during the observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day on November 1 and 2.
The PNP said it would deploy personnel at transportation hubs, including airports, seaports and bus terminals amid expectations of increased passenger traffic.
Authorities expect travel activity to increase on the evening of October 29, with a more significant increase anticipated on the afternoon of October 30.

articles.title: Chinese ships seen near PH fuel distribution to fishermen at Scarborough Shoal — PCG
articles.summary: Chinese coast guard and navy ships were spotted near Scarborough Shoal on Tuesday, October 27, while Philippine government vessels handed out fuel to Filipino fishermen, the Philippine Coast Guard…

blocks.text: October 28, 2026 | 2:56pm

the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) successfully conducted a fuel distribution mission for Filipino fishermen in the vicinity of Bajo de Masinloc under the Kadiwa ng Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda (KBBM) Program, Oct. 27, 2026.
Philippine Coast Guard

MANILA, Philippines — Chinese coast guard and navy ships were spotted near Scarborough Shoal on Tuesday, October 27, while Philippine government vessels handed out fuel to Filipino fishermen, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
A PCG aircraft flying over the area saw China Coast Guard and People's Liberation Army Navy vessels "in the approaches" to the shoal.
The PCG also spotted a Chinese research vessel operating near the shoal.
The Chinese ships did not interfere with the mission, which was completed "without any untoward incident," PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela said.
A similar fuel mission at the shoal in July saw CCG ships fire water cannons at Philippine government vessels on two straight days, July 23 and 24.
China's coast guard said then it had driven away two Philippine vessels it accused of violating Chinese sovereignty.
On Tuesday, October 27, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel MV Mamalakaya delivered the fuel for Filipino fishers in the area, as escorted by the PCG ship BRP Malapascua.
"Upon the arrival of MV Mamalakaya, Filipino fishing boats already operating in the traditional fishing ground, numbering 40 to 50, approached the vessel and lined up to receive fuel," the PCG said.
The shoal lies about 124 nautical miles off Masinloc, Zambales, inside the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.
China has controlled it since a 2012 standoff and has kept ships there since.
A 2016 arbitral ruling found China had unlawfully blocked Filipino fishing at the shoal, but Beijing has never recognized the ruling.

articles.title: PNP: 3 persons of interest in Laos-PH drug smuggling have yet to appear to authorities
articles.summary: Three persons of interest in the investigation into an alleged drug smuggling operation involving Laos and the Philippines have yet to appear before authorities, the Philippine National Police (PNP)…

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 2:54pm

Three persons of interest in the investigation into an alleged drug smuggling operation involving Laos and the Philippines have yet to appear before authorities, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said on Wednesday.
“Meron pa pong tatlo hindi nagpapakita,” PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said at a press conference.
(There are still three who are not showing up.)

“We will give you all the details and of course, lalo na kapag umabot na po tayo sa point where we have transmitted the case or we have filed the case ay doon po natin malalaman lahat ng lumabas po,” he added.
(We will give you all the details and of course, especially when we reach the point where we have transmitted the case or we have filed the case, we will know all the results.)
Co said the three individuals have yet to respond to the call to appear before the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) and provide their statements.
Authorities are urging them to cooperate with investigators, warning that failure to appear could lead to the filing of an indirect contempt case.
The CIDG is handling the investigation and the gathering of statements from persons of interest, following a case conference between the PNP and the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA).
The two agencies have agreed on the division of tasks as they pursue the investigation, according to Co.
Investigators are conducting criminal and financial investigations with assistance from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
The PNP said authorities are currently evaluating the evidence for the joint transmittal of the case by the PNP and PDEA.
Investigators are also awaiting the official transmission of case files from Laos and Malaysia.
On October 1, Lao authorities thwarted P3.5 billion in illegal drugs on a private plane headed to the Philippines.
The PNP issued subpoenas to 11 persons of interest. — BAP, GMA News

articles.summary: Now back at the helm of the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Secretary Vince Dizon on Wednesday warned motorists against violating traffic rules, stressing that a driver's license is a privilege,…

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 2:48pm

Now back at the helm of the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Secretary Vince Dizon on Wednesday warned motorists against violating traffic rules, stressing that a driver's license is a privilege, not a right.
Dizon returned as DOTr chief this week after switching posts with Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez, who now heads the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

“Sinimulan na namin ni Sec. Banoy 'yan saka si Asec. [Markus] Lacanilao. Talagang istrikto siya diyan na kailangan talaga, kapag ang lisensya, pribilehiyo 'yan, hindi 'yan karapatan. Ibig sabihin, kung pribilehiyo 'yan, kailangan sumunod ka sa alituntunin ng tamang pagmamaneho. 'Pag ikaw ay lumabag, pasensiya na. Tatanggalin namin 'yung pribilehiyo mong 'yan,” Dizon said in an interview on Balitanghali.

(We started this with Secretary Banoy and Assistant Secretary Lacanilao, who is very strict about enforcing the rule that a driver's license is a privilege, not a right. This means motorists must follow proper driving rules. If you violate them, we're sorry, but we will take away that privilege.)
Dizon said the government should prioritize not only motorists but also commuters and pedestrians who struggle with their daily journeys to school and work.

“Ang kabilin-bilinan ng Pangulo natin, kailangan commuter at mga pedestrians at ang mga kababayan nating araw-araw nahihirapan sa pagpasok sa eskwela, pagpasok sa trabaho, sila naman ang gawing prayoridad,” Dizon said.
(The President's directive is to prioritize commuters, pedestrians, and our fellow Filipinos who struggle every day to get to school and work.)
Asked about fixers at the Land Transportation Office (LTO), Dizon said Lacanilao had also begun implementing reforms to address the problem.

“'Di ba dapat modern na tayo? Dapat hindi na pumipila ng mahaba, hindi na nahihirapan, hindi kailangan magbayad ng extra para mapabilis ang papeles sa pagkuha ng lisensya, pag-register ng sasakyan ngayong panahon na ito, pero nangyayari pa rin,” Dizon said.

(Shouldn't we be modern by now? People should no longer have to wait in long lines or go through difficulties, and they should not have to pay extra to expedite their driver's license applications or vehicle registrations. Yet these practices still persist.) — Jean Mangaluz/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: We asked you - what do you want from the Burnham government’s first budget?
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: First Edition readers and people struggling with the cost of living tell us what the government could do to improve their lives

Good morning. Don’t expect anything…

blocks.text: Good morning. Don’t expect anything radical. This, the Treasury has been at pains to tell us, will be a very “low-key” budget. After weeks of speculation from journalists, a flurry of press releases from thinktanks, and a photoshoot with an obligatory red box, the chancellor, John Healey, will announce the details of the Burnham government’s first budget in the Commons today at 12:30pm.

Healey has been selling this as a series of measures designed to relieve pressure on low- and middle-income households under the mangled tagline of “breathing space for today, fresh hope for the future”. Many of the proposals have already been briefed, and their modesty is a sign of the constraints – both real and self-imposed – that his government faces. He has rejected calls to raise capital gains tax or lower the mansion tax and has promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules, while the Iran war has increased the cost of borrowing and eroded his spending power.

Voters might be hoping for something transformative from a government that risks presiding over the worst parliament for living standards on record. That’s the impression I got from First Edition readers and people struggling with the cost of living, who I spoke to for this morning’s newsletter about what they’d like to see from today’s budget. First, here are the headlines.
Five big stories

items: Israeli elections | Israel could be in for weeks of political haggling after exit polls and partial official results showed neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by former general Gadi Eisenkot had won enough seats to form a government.

Energy | The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.

Middle East | A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.

UK news | A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English.

Brazil | The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled Brazil and is on his way to the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘It’s not going to be ending 40 years of neoliberalism’

blocks.caption: A shop advertises a mid season sale in Wolverhampton, United Kingdom.  Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

blocks.text: There was some detectable grumbling earlier this week over the lack of information about this budget compared with those of Rachel Reeves, and Healey has made much of the “military-style protocols” that have allegedly stopped the Treasury’s secrets from leaking out. But it seems more likely that there hasn’t been much to leak. “It’s going to be a far smaller budget than last year,” Kiran Stacey, the Guardian’s policy editor, told me on Monday. “It’s not going to be ending 40 years of neoliberalism.”

We’ve already covered some of its content: Patrick Butler and Pippa Crerar wrote yesterday on the government’s plan to abolish the detested rule that has plunged unpaid carers into debt (which the Guardian exposed last year). The government was criticised yesterday for pausing the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage, paid to people under 21, with the more generous “national living wage” for older workers, and has also announced a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living pressures facing UK households. That is expected to include support for poorer families with energy bills this winter and to pledge energy market reforms aimed at bringing down bills for all households in the longer term.

The extent of those pressures is remarkable. StepChange, the UK’s largest debt advice charity, pulled together some figures for this morning’s First Edition that show the average household arrears debt for their clients increased from £2,833 to £4,345 between 2022 and 2025. “In the late 2000s, people would primarily come to us with consumer credit debt,” a spokesperson from the charity told me. “But one in two people who come to us now have energy debt. These pressures are completely new.”
*** What could the government do to address energy bills?

A number of readers told First Edition that energy bills are their major concern. Michael works for a small property company, and rents a three-bedroom bungalow in Winchester where he lives with his three children. It’s draughty, and he spends about £165 a month on electricity and gas, which will increase this winter. “I think about the cost of everything now,” he tells me. “Will I get enough money to be able to afford this? Will I have enough when the rent is due?”

Healey has been considering making the warm homes discount, a £150 annual reduction to electricity bills for people in receipt of benefits, more generous. But Michael doesn’t qualify for this, since he doesn’t receive benefits. After tax, his monthly income is between £2,500 and £3,000, and his rent is £1,800 a month, leaving him at most £300 each week (in a good month) to cover the living costs of four people. The warm homes discount is targeted at the most needy and does nothing for people further up the income spectrum who are still struggling.

“Alongside funded measures to provide immediate relief, the government needs a structural plan to reduce energy bills over the medium term,” Mathew Lawrence, the director of Common Wealth, a thinktank that has been cited as an influence on Burnham’s government, tells me. One idea would be an “energy guarantee”, a protected bloc of energy priced at pre-crisis levels (as Kiran reported earlier this month, energy officials are working up more radical changes that could be introduced after the budget). But Healey has ruled out some of the tax changes that could help fund this type of policy. “So decisions on tax have limited the government’s scope for action on bills,” Mathew says.
What about food bills?

A persistent causes of stress for Michael is the rising cost of food. “Once something goes up in price, it never comes down again,” he says. This is well evidenced: one report from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, published in May, observed that when food prices in the UK have risen during crises such as the pandemic, they have either fallen slowly or incompletely, or have stayed the same indefinitely.

One of the proposals the government announced on Monday is the removal of import tariffs on products including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins. But the impact on household budgets will be pretty minimal; the Treasury estimates it will save £21 on the average yearly food shop. For Michael, who tries to limit his weekly food shop in Aldi to £80, this will barely make a dent.
What will the government do about housing costs?

This was another concern that cropped up among First Edition readers. Sue, from west Kent, wants the chancellor to announce more council housing. Burnham has committed Labour to the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar decade, and Healey is expected to announce a further £1bn in funding for this. He’ll also likely provide more details of the Your First Home scheme designed to help first-time buyers get on the property ladder, a new version of the Help to Buy scheme, which pushed up house prices and made property developers inordinately rich.

The impact of both of these measures will only be felt in the longer term. A more immediate solution would be linking local housing allowance, which has been frozen since 2024, to rents. The Resolution Foundation finds that more than 900,000 private rented households on universal credit face a shortfall between their rent and their housing allowance, averaging £158 a month for a family renting a two-bedroom home.
Finally, what about fuel prices?

Pat, from Aberdeen, told us that she’d like to see the government reduce fuel prices. The rising cost of petrol is penalising people who rely on their cars to get around, and the government has announced that it will be continuing the freeze on fuel duty, the tax levied on every litre of petrol or diesel, which Rishi Sunak announced in 2022.

But maintaining the freeze on fuel duty will largely help higher-income households, who drive more, while depriving the government of a revenue source. “Obviously some people on low incomes have to drive a lot. But they’re also struggling with the cost of living at large,” says Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation. “So instead of using this rather blunt instrument, it would be better to find other ways to help poorer households, particularly with more action on energy bills.”
What else we’ve been reading

blocks.caption: Students celebrate after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Belgrade, Serbia, 26 October 2026.  Photograph: Uros Arsic/Reuters

items: After writing about the Serbian elections last week, I was glad to read Aleksandar Matković’s thoughtful analysis of their outcome and what weary European democracies can learn from the triumphant ‘bunch of students’. Libby
I found Zoe Williams’ column hilarious and self-knowing – on how the people who see you least may just know you best. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

Our Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan, has been following calls for a full apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade from King Charles – this thorough piece sets out what’s a stake as he begins his tour of the region. Libby

Why won’t MPs tax the rich? This incredibly insightful piece by Faiza Shaheen asked politicians that exact question – and their answers provided useful insight on how to push the dial. Well worth a read. Poppy

After his Orwell prize-winning book Poverty Safari was referenced by Andy Burnham in his first speech in Scotland as Labour leader, writer and activist Darren McGarvey doesn’t pull punches in this interview with the National. Libby

Sport

blocks.caption: Photograph: Jon Super/Reuters

blocks.text: Football | Conor Haughey scored the winning penalty in Fleetwood’s 5-3 shootout win against 10-man Arsenal, after the Carabao Cup fourth round tie finished 1-1.
Football | Michael Carrick has been given the chance to save his job by turning Manchester United’s results around, with the head coach remaining in place for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea.
Cricket | Australia fought back in a rollercoaster start to the deciding Test against South Africa, as hosts all out for 329.
The front pages

blocks.caption: frontpage29oct Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “Healey targets cost of living crisis in budget for a ‘difficult moment’”, is the Guardian’s splash today. The Times leads on “Healey to cut energy bills by scrapping green levies”, the i Paper has “Burnham to target rising energy bills in high-stakes first Budget”, and the FT’s take is “Healey puts energy reform at centre of Budget aimed at steadying nerves”. Still on the budget, the Mail has £6 billion budget benefits bonanza”, the Mirror writes “A budget for workers”, and the Express says “Kemi: Labour is coming for your pay packets”.
Elsewhere, the Telegraph leads on “King: Slavery was a ‘great suffering’”, the Sun says “Arise Sir Harry”, and Metro has “Wife ‘victim of a sick fantasy’”.
The Latest

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win

Harry Kane is the men’s Ballon d’Or winner for 2026, the first Englishman to win the trophy in 25 years. At a lavish ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London, Kane unexpectedly won ahead of co-favourites Lamine Yamal of Barcelona and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid. In a contest that has been critiqued for promoting individualism and celebrity in sport, Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s chief sports writer, Barney Ronay, about the symbolism of Kane’s win.
Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron

blocks.caption: Illustration: Ella Baron/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Younger users have become increasingly aware of the downsides of social media. Photograph: Iryna Khabliuk/Alamy

blocks.text: Amid the unrelenting tales of woe regarding social media’s impact on young minds, some enterprising gen-Z’s are working on fixes for their peers. As younger users become increasingly wearied by the attention-splicing, joy-sapping demands of social media, a growing number of companies are offering means to digitally detox while individuals are likewise getting creative.
Nineteen-year-old Shreya Nallamothu, for example, a computer science student at Duke University, has invented her own DIY Brick device to block selected apps.

“Everyone deserves to have a good relationship with technology, and it shouldn’t be cost-prohibitive,” Nallamothu says. “Often the tech companies’ best interests aren’t in the users’ best interests. Social media has gotten away from what good technology can do, and people have noticed.”
Bored at work?

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo warns Lalamove of contempt over repeated hearing absences
articles.summary: Senator Raffy Tulfo on Wednesday warned delivery and logistics platform Lalamove that it could be cited for contempt after repeatedly failing to attend Senate hearings on road safety concerns.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 2:36pm
Senator Raffy Tulfo on Wednesday warned delivery and logistics platform Lalamove that it could be cited for contempt after repeatedly failing to attend Senate hearings on road safety concerns.

During a hearing of the Senate Committee on Public Services, which he chairs, Tulfo ordered the issuance of a show-cause order requiring the company to explain why it should not be cited for contempt.

The committee secretary said an invitation had been sent to Lalamove, but no representative attended the hearing. Tulfo said this was the third consecutive time the company had failed to appear before the panel.

“Send a show-cause order to them, why they should not be cited in contempt. Because this is the third time palaging nag-iisnub sa hearing itong mga taga-Lalamove. I don’t know kung anong meron sa utak nila bakit nila ini-isnub itong mga hearing three times in a row,” Tulfo said.

(Send them a show-cause order asking why they should not be cited for contempt. This is the third time that Lalamove has snubbed the hearings. I don’t know what’s going on in their minds—why they are snubbing these hearings three times in a row now.)

Lalamove is an on-demand delivery and logistics platform founded in Hong Kong in 2013. It entered the Philippine market in 2016 and connects individuals and businesses with drivers through its mobile application for the delivery of documents, parcels and larger cargo.

The company offers various vehicle options, including motorcycles, cars, vans and trucks, for deliveries of different sizes. It also provides logistics services to micro, small and medium enterprises and larger businesses.
Lalamove operates in the Philippines through Lalamove Philippines Inc. and Lalamove Technology Philippines Inc., according to its corporate entity listing.
Tulfo also warned that he would seek an arrest warrant against the company's owner if Lalamove continued to ignore a subpoena.
“Kapag hindi pa rin umattend sa subpoena natin, then magpalabas ka ng warrant of arrest. The owner, sa pinaka-may-ari mismo,” he said.
(If they still fail to attend after receiving our subpoena, then issue an arrest warrant—specifically for the company's owner.)
The hearing tackled concerns involving driver welfare, fair compensation and the security of items handled by Lalamove.
GMA News Online has reached out to Lalamove for comment and will update this story once it responds.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: PH spotlights South China Sea, ‘fragmenting world’ in ASEAN defense chiefs’ meeting
articles.summary: Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun skips the ADMM-Plus meeting, as bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing hit their tensest note yet

blocks.text: Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro delivers opening remarks during the 20th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) at the Mactan Expo in Cebu, Philippines 28 October 2026.
Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun skips the ADMM-Plus meeting, as bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing hit their tensest note yet

items: Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. emphasized the importance of unity among ASEAN members despite differing ties with China, advocating for peaceful resolution of disputes, particularly in the South China Sea.

The ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting in Cebu will address regional security, disaster risk reduction, and cooperation on critical infrastructure, food, and energy security, with participation from defense ministers of Southeast Asia and dialogue partners.

Teodoro's leadership comes amid tense PH-China relations, with the Philippines strengthening defense ties with the US and Japan, while navigating the complexities of ASEAN's diverse relationships with China.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines — Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. told Southeast Asian defense chiefs, whose countries have widely varying ties with superpower China, that the bloc should “not allow differences to divide us from within.”

“ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] was founded on the belief that our strength lies in our diversity. We must therefore not allow our differences to divide us from within, and where such differences exist, including in the South China Sea, we shall settle them through peaceful and legal means,” said Teodoro, chairman of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting, to open the event on Wednesday, October 28.

Regional security, as well as bloc cooperation over issues like disaster risk reduction, will be among the key issues defense officials are expected to tackle in meetings and sideline events from October 28 to 29 at the Mactan Expo in Lapu-Lapu City.

Ministers, as well as working groups, are also expected to tackle protection of underwater critical infrastructure, cooperation for food and energy security, and preparedness for the super El Niño and its possible effects on security.

blocks.caption: PH spotlights South China Sea, ‘fragmenting world’ in ASEAN defense chiefs’ meeting

blocks.text: ADMM and the ADMM-Plus is an annual gathering of defense ministers from Southeast Asia and “plus countries” or ADMM dialogue partners Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. It is the largest defense diplomacy gathering in ASEAN for the calendar year.

Aside from all 11 defense chiefs from Southeast Asia, their counterparts for almost all plus countries, including US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Japan Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, are participating in the meetings.

blocks.caption: Hegseth likely to face questions on US role in Indo-Pacific at ASEAN summit in Cebu

blocks.text: As chair of ADMM, Teodoro will preside over all meetings, including two separate “informal meetings” with the US and Japan.
China’s Dong Jun will not be attending ADMM+. Beijing will instead be represented by its defense attache assigned to the Chinese embassy in Manila.
Cebu province has hosted several meetings under the Philippines’ chairmanship, including the first Foreign Ministers’ meeting, and the Summit in May.

“In a fragmenting world, our internal stability and intra-ASEAN unity are vital, perhaps even, in the future, existential. For it is only when we are united that we can effectively uphold ASEAN centrality and the principles that bind us, such as mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes, and the renunciation of the threat or use of force,” said Teodoro, in remarks that preceded a direct mention of the South China Sea.
While disputes over and tensions in the critical waterway won’t be the center of discussions in Cebu, they certainly backdrop the Philippines’ chairmanship both of ASEAN and ADMM.

Teodoro, among the loudest critics of Beijing in the Philippine government, is barred from entering and transacting in China over his statements against the Asian superpower. Just weeks before ADMM, China’s ambassador to Manila was criticized for saying the Philippines should be thankful that they do not use force in its disputes — a statement made in reaction to Teodoro’s assertion that it was Beijing who was causing trouble in the region.

China claims almost all of the South China Sea, based on a supposed historical claim that a landmark 2016 Arbitral Award deemed invalid. Their claim overlaps with maritime claims and entitlements of several ASEAN members, including the Philippines.

In the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, those overlapping claims have meant recurring confrontations between Chinese and Philippine maritime forces in some areas and features.
Tensions in the South China Sea is a concern for ASEAN not only because several members are claimants. The waterway is where up to a third of global trade passes through.

“ASEAN was founded on the belief that our strength lies in our diversity. We must therefore not allow our differences to divide us from within, and where such differences exist, including in the South China Sea, we shall settle them through peaceful and legal means,” said Teodoro.

blocks.caption: ADMM CHAIR. Philippines’ Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. waits for his counterparts’ arrival during the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM), Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Cebu, central Philippines.

blocks.text: As chair of ADMM, it’s the Philippines who steers the agenda. It’s almost no surprise that in Cebu, the Philippines is hosting two “informal meetings” with treaty-ally United States and close partner Japan.

Manila’s defense and security ties are deepest and most developed with Washington DC and Tokyo. The two countries are its staunchest partners in South China Sea issues and in its push to modernize the Philippine military. Manila is the first recipient of Japan’s Official Security Assistance (OSA). The US has allocated over $2.5 billion over five years in foreign military financing for the Philippines.

Teodoro is also expected to host a quadrilateral meeting between Hegseth, Koizumi, and Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles, a grouping known colloquially as the SQUAD.
The Philippines’ defense engagements — both with traditional and new partners — is spurred, in no small way, by maritime tensions with China.

In ASEAN, member states have varying degrees of closeness and cooperation with Beijing. It’s a difference that’s made cohesion a challenge, especially in a bloc that puts centrality and unanimity at the center of its decision-making and policy-making process. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Australia must ‘re-win the argument for democratic politics’ in wake of Haines incident, Alastair Campbell says
articles.summary:
Tony Blair’s former spokesperson says attacks on UK MPs did not bring about lasting cultural change and overheated rhetoric quickly returned to politics

  • Get our

blocks.text: Tony Blair’s former communications guru, Alastair Campbell, says the UK political system was too quick to revert to overheated rhetoric and polarisation after attacks on MPs, urging politicians to “re-win the argument for democratic politics”.

More than a week after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly targeted in an attack outside her electorate office in northern Victoria, causing her to lose both legs, Campbell said the tenor of political debate in Australia should better reflect Haines’ own approach.

Speaking to the Guardian’s Australian Politics podcast on Wednesday, the commentator said the killings of British MPs Jo Cox, David Amess and former politician Ann Widdecombe had not brought about lasting change in political culture.
“They were followed by everybody saying the right thing about how our political debate culture had to change, about how we had to address online hate and polarisation, all this stuff,” he said.
“But it didn’t take long before we kind of got right back into it. So I think it is about how we genuinely try and generate a different way of talking to each other and about each other now.”
A 43-year-old man has been charged over the alleged attack on Haines and the incident continues to be investigated by police.
The co-host of popular podcast The Rest is Politics, Campbell said Haines’ eventual return to parliament would help bring about change.
“It’s very rare these days that an individual act or incident lasts more than half a news cycle, and so we just move on. I think remembering is so important.

“In a way, the fact that she is still with us and is going to still be part of the political debate, maybe that will help people … that people will see that that is the consequence of the actions that were taken against her.”
A former journalist, Campbell is the author of more than 20 books, including diaries documenting his years working inside 10 Downing Street.
He is due to visit Australia for a speaking tour next month.
Campbell said politicians and the media should reflect on how they speak to everyday people, and why their professions are so poorly trusted.
after newsletter promotion

“It’s made more difficult at the moment because you’ve got Donald Trump in America as the loudest, most talked about politician on the planet, and he represents a lot of the things that I think we don’t want in our politics.
“We’ve got to re-win the argument for democratic politics because it’s under a lot of pressure right now,” he said.
Discussing the rise of populist politics, Campbell said the world was still struggling to grasp the effects of the 2008 global financial crisis.

“If I think of one thing that maybe ties the rise of Trump to Brexit, to the protests that we’re seeing in different parts of Europe, I think is that we haven’t really come to terms with the consequences of the financial crisis, and the sense that there was socialism for the banks who caused it, and austerity for the people, and the people who are still struggling to see their living standards rise.
“That, ultimately I think, is a big driver of what the Americans call affordability, what we call cost of living, just the sense that people don’t feel that they’re able to get on.”
Campbell revealed he occasionally watches clips of Paul Keating’s parliamentary attacks as Australia’s prime minister in the 1990s.
The bestselling author’s latest book is Persevilience: The Word the World Needs Now, published by Allen and Unwin.

articles.title: Fuel surcharge rises to Level 17 for November 1-15, 2026 flights
articles.summary: Air travelers should brace for higher airfares for flights booked between November 1 and 15, 2026 as the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) raised the fuel surcharge level.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 2:12pm
Air travelers should brace for higher airfares for flights booked between November 1 and 15, 2026 as the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) raised the fuel surcharge level.
In an advisory, the CAB said the fuel surcharge level for the second half of November was upgraded to Level 17, from Level 16 in the October 16 to 31, 2026 period.
Under Level 17, airlines may impose a fuel surcharge ranging from P559 to P1,635 for domestic flights and from P1,846.10 to P13,726.58 for international flights, depending on the distance.
These are higher than the Level 16 surcharge rates for the October 16-31 period at P525 to P1,535 for domestic flights and P1,733.76 to P12,891.29 for international flights.
The fuel surcharge is an additional fee that airlines may collect on top of the base fare to help offset the impact of fluctuations in fuel prices.
The CAB implements a 15-day fuel price monitoring and surcharge cycle to help mitigate the impact of fuel price increases on air travel costs.

The agency added airlines intending to impose or collect the fuel surcharge must file their applications with the Office of the Executive Director on or before the start of the applicable effectivity period. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: DPWH to scrutinize flagged insertions in 2027 budget
articles.summary: The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) will scrutinize alleged insertions of infrastructure projects in the House of Representatives-approved 2027 budget to determine whether they are…

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 2:04pm

The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) will scrutinize alleged insertions of infrastructure projects in the House of Representatives-approved 2027 budget to determine whether they are justified, newly installed Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez said on Wednesday.

The agency will check whether the projects are backed by supporting documents, master plans, feasibility studies and coordination with local government units (LGUs), Lopez said in an interview with Balitanghali.
“May mga pagpupulong na po kami sa mga susunod na araw. Sisikapin naming suriin kung ano ang mga proyektong binanggit at kung may sapat na batayan ang mga ito,” Lopez said.
(We have meetings scheduled in the coming days. We will scrutinize the projects that were mentioned and determine whether they have sufficient basis.)

The watchdog People’s Budget Coalition recently flagged around 6,000 proposed projects involving multipurpose buildings and local access roads, saying these appeared to have contributed to reduced funding for foreign-assisted projects.
Lopez thanked the watchdog for monitoring government spending, saying citizens’ groups played an important role in helping the government through their vigilance.
Lopez assumed the DPWH post on Monday, swapping positions with Vince Dizon, who took over the Department of Transportation (DOTr). Dizon had previously served as DPWH chief.
At a press conference the following day, Dizon handed Lopez a thick stack of documents. Asked about their contents, Lopez declined to provide specific details but said they contained complaints.

The DPWH has been at the center of a multibillion-peso corruption controversy during the administration of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. following revelations of an alleged kickback scheme involving flood control projects and public officials.
The alleged scheme involved inserting infrastructure projects into the budget, inflating project costs and manipulating bidding processes to award contracts to favored contractors.

These contractors would then allegedly carry out substandard construction to make room for kickbacks intended for various recipients, including lawmakers and personnel of the DPWH and in some cases, the Commission on Audit (COA).

Lopez also said he planned to revisit Bulacan, which emerged as a focal point of the controversy. Former DPWH engineers assigned to district offices in the province have admitted to helping funnel public funds through ghost projects.
“Kailangan naming tutukan kung ano po ang nangyari dito sa Bulacan. Sa mga susunod na araw, kailangan naming bumalik kasama si Sec. Vince (Dizon) at kailangang ayusin,” Lopez said.
(We need to focus on what happened here in Bulacan. In the coming days, we need to return with Secretary Vince and address the problems.)
Dizon, who took over the DPWH following the resignation of Manuel Bonoan amid questions of command responsibility, said the agency continued to need public assistance in addressing corruption.
He urged citizens’ groups, religious organizations and ordinary Filipinos to regularly report alleged irregularities involving DPWH personnel across the country.

“Hiningi natin ang tulong ng ating mga partner citizens’ groups, ang simbahan at ang mga ordinaryong Pilipino, na magsumite regularly sa atin ng mga report ng mga kawani ng DPWH sa iba't ibang lugar sa Pilipinas,” Dizon said.
(We have asked our partner citizens’ groups, the Church and ordinary Filipinos to regularly submit reports to us about DPWH personnel in various parts of the Philippines.)— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: What to expect from John Healey’s first budget: who wins, who pays?
articles.summary:
Struggling households, new homebuyers and small shops stand to gain, while banks and online marketplaces could face higher levies

John Healey will present his first budget on Wednesday,…

blocks.text: John Healey will present his first budget on Wednesday, which will set the tone for Andy Burnham’s premiership.

Despite the chancellor’s promises in the summer that the tax and spending event would not be beset by the leaks that preceded those of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, both official and unofficial sources have indicated much of what Healey is likely to announce. Here’s what to expect:
How much money is there?

Healey will allocate about £1.42tn this year on day-to-day spending and public investment. About £100bn of this will go on debt interest after a rise in the interest rate the government pays to multidecade highs.

Most of this increase can be blamed on the Gulf conflict launched by the US and Israel at the end of February, which has taken the oil price to above $110 a barrel and the price of gas to levels not seen since late 2022.

Government borrowing in this financial year has fallen compared with 2025-26, but not by as much as the Office for Budget Responsibility estimated in March, mainly owing to higher debt financing. Healey is spending about £1bn a month more than forecast.

Those costs mean the buffer of £24bn built up in the last tax-raising budget is likely to have halved to £12bn, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank. The Treasury would be more comfortable having this headroom at about £15bn, according to economists at ING.
It’s a headache the chancellor could do without when he needs extra cash to fund cost of living measures, but also higher defence spending and the prime minister’s pet projects, such as devolution.
What does he want to spend money on?
The chancellor has promised to give consumers and businesses “breathing space” with a range of measures to help with soaring costs.

Everyday fixes: This is what the Treasury calls its proposals to help struggling households. They include an extension of parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year worth £388, including self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out.

Healey will also end the carer’s allowance cliff-edge, so unpaid carers no longer lose more than their allowance once they hit their weekly earnings limit. He will also remove import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, to reduce their shop prices.

Energy bills: The chancellor is planning to spend more than £1bn to help poorer households struggling with soaring gas and electricity bills, with the bulk going towards an expansion of the existing Warm Home Discount. An additional £100 could be added to this £150 means-tested yearly rebate, funded by taxes rather than billpayers as the current discount is.

Burnham has already suspended VAT on electricity bills for six months and said last week he had asked the Treasury to explore abolishing standing charges on gas bills. These are now expected that they will disappear.

Help for first-time homebuyers: The budget will provide more detail of how the “your first home” scheme – first announced at Labour’s annual party conference last month – will work in practice. The revamped version of the Tories’ “help to buy” programme will give first-time buyers a 20% equity loan towards a new-build home, with an initial interest-free period and a minimum deposit of just 2.5%.

Defence: Healey aims to plug a £4.7bn gap in the government’s defence investment plan, inherited from Keir Starmer, with cuts to other departmental budgets ikely to be the main source of funding. However, despite resigning in June over raising defence spending to 3% of GDP, a roadmap showing how that target will be hit by 2030 will now not come until the spending review next year.
What taxes could Healey raise?

Healey is unable to increase rates of income tax, national insurance, and VAT without breaking manifesto commitments and has promised to stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules and not borrow to fund day-to-day spending. However, these are some of the revenue-raising measures he’s reportedly considering.

Bank tax: The Guardian revealed this month that the budget’s main revenue-raising measure is expected to be a levy on ​banks. The sector’s resistance has been undermined by a run of bumper quarterly profits on the back of higher interest rates, culminating in HSBC revealing on Tuesday that its had risen 32% to about £7.2bn.
Jeremy Hunt cut the bank surcharge – a supplement to corporation tax – from 8% to 3% ahead of the last election and one option on the table is reversing this cut to raise more than £2bn a year.

Taxes on online sellers: There has been strong lobbying from Labour backbenchers and unions to increase the taxes paid by online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay. The former Burnham adviser Andy Haldane used a Guardian interview to urge Healey to “level the playing field” with physical stores. One proposal reportedly drawn up would raise up to an extra £1bn by forcing them to collect VAT on behalf of large-scale sellers based in the UK as well as those overseas.

That money could be used to fund a cut in business rates paid by small high-street shops, possibly in the form of an increase to the threshold at which they start paying from £12,000 to £18,000. This would help the “bloody-minded entrepreneurs” that Healey has said he wants to support.
Other taxes: Alcohol duty is likely to rise in line with the retail prices index (RPI) measure of inflation, which will increase the tax on a pint from 50p to 52p.
What taxes is he expected not to touch?

Mansion tax: Treasury officials have played down speculation of significant changes to Reeves’s measure, which imposes an annual charge worth up to £7,500 on properties valued at more than £2m from April 2028. The chancellor was understood to be considering lowering the threshold to £1.5m, but London MPs have pushed back and are confident Healey has ruled out the move.

Capital gains tax: The chancellor has rejected calls by senior Labour MPs to raise CGT to the same levels as income tax. Some of his cabinet colleagues have called for the tax rates on income and asset gains to be equalised. However, influential figures, such as the former Treasury minister Jim O’Neill have pushed back, saying it would harm the incentives for wealth creators.

Fuel duty A longstanding freeze in fuel duty had already been extended to the end of the year, but it is due to rise by 3p a litre in January and 2p a litre in March. The default is also for an increase in line with RPI from April. However, with petrol and diesel at near-record highs the chancellor is expected to continue the freeze. Extending for an additional year could cost up to £2.7bn, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, while keeping it to 2029-30 would cost another £4bn.

Inheritance tax: While the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch has proposed raising the tax-free threshold from £325,000 to £500,000 and excluding family homes from the calculation, Labour is not expected to propose any changes of its own.
Other measures

Devolution: Spreading decision-making to the far reaches of England is a major element of Burnham’s plans for economic growth. Healey will offer a £150m funding boost to help mayoralties and local authorities scale up for the new work they will carry out.

In addition there will be a £1.5bn borrowing facility. The package will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.
Golden visas: Healey is understood to have scrapped plans for a new visa route to the UK aimed at wealthy people from overseas that were explored by the Treasury earlier in the year.

articles.title: Volunteer, 78, says Reform official likened her to Nazi collaborator for teaching asylum seekers English
articles.summary:
Mair Godley claims Essex councillor Carl Johnson told her she was ‘facilitating the invasion’ by giving language lessons

A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused…

blocks.text: A 78-year-old volunteer has claimed a Reform UK councillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English.

Mair Godley and her husband, Nick, 77, a former chair of Wethersfield parish council, live near the former Wethersfield military base in Essex, where the Home Office accommodates hundreds of asylum seekers.
The couple said the accusations were made against Mair Godley at a parish council meeting on 14 October.

blocks.caption: The former Wethersfield military base. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Reform took over control of Essex county council after the elections in May 2026, ending 25 years of Conservative control. The Reform councillor, Carl Johnson, attended the meeting to update members of the parish council about local issues for which it has responsibility, including repairing potholes and “Operation Vanguard”, which involves private security guards patrolling Essex town centres.
Wethersfield is the larger of two former military sites the Home Office uses to provide mass accommodation for asylum seekers. The other is at Crowborough in Sussex.

Nick Godley challenged Johnson at the meeting about the potholes and whether Operation Vanguard was needed to protect local people against asylum seekers. He said crime and antisocial behaviour incidents in nearby Braintree, where asylum seekers sometimes go to, were low.

blocks.caption: Temporary housing units at the former Wethersfield military base. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: In response, Johnson asked if anyone in the room had been helping the migrants at Wethersfield and “facilitating the invasion”. Mair Godley said she had previously volunteered to help teach English to the asylum seekers at the facility.

Johnson then reportedly said that by doing so she might as well have been helping Germany during second world war. He said he didn’t want to bring his daughter up to be raped and murdered by asylum seekers.

In a Facebook post the week before the parish council meeting, Johnson had written that people who enter the country “illegally” received things including clothing and accommodation for free while “the rest of us” had to pay for items. “I have never known a country to actively facilitate its own invasion and population replacement,” he wrote. “This is treason.”
According to the draft minutes of the parish council meeting seen by the Guardian the discussion became heated and Johnson was asked to leave the meeting to “restore order”.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: An aerial view of part of the former Wethersfield military base. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Mair Godley said: “I’m nearly 79 years old. I felt violated by his comments. How dare he say that to me? I certainly told him at the meeting, ‘you are not wanted here’. He has left a really bad taste.”

Nick Godley said he had had a “fairly challenging” discussion with Johnson about Operation Vanguard. It was after he had raised concerns that it had been introduced without consultation that Johnson accused Mair Godley of being akin to a Nazi collaborator by helping asylum seekers to learn English.
“It was a member of the public who attended the meeting who suggested forcibly that he should leave. Cllr Johnson’s behaviour was shocking,” said Nick Godley.
He has lodged a formal complaint about Johnson’s comments at the meeting with Essex county council.
A spokesperson for the council said: “We comment on complaints made at a point where they have been investigated and a finding of a breach has been made, but not before that point.”
Reform UK and Johnson have not responded to repeated requests for comment.

articles.title: Jim Chalmers is blaming Australia’s accelerating inflation on Trump – but voters aren’t buying it
articles.summary:
As next week’s all-but certain rate rise looms, there is one thing we can all agree on: the end of war in the Middle East can’t come soon enough

Jim Chalmers is blaming the latest shocking…

blocks.text: Jim Chalmers is blaming the latest shocking inflation figures on the worsening Middle East conflict, and he has a point.
The trouble is, voters aren’t buying what the treasurer is selling.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said that the 9.4% jump in fuel costs in September was largely responsible for inflation accelerating from 4% to 4.3%.
Petrol and diesel prices were on average 24% higher than a year earlier, the data show.
We are clearly paying an economic price for Trump’s pointless and damaging war on Iran – and you can’t pin that on the government, whatever your political leanings.
Then there’s the sudden boom in spending on datacentres, which is pouring money into an economy that is already struggling to deliver the workers and materials needed to build homes and roads.
Again, this is driven by the global rush by tech companies to put in place the infrastructure to power their artificial intelligence revolution.

Earlier in the day, Michele Bullock, the RBA’s governor, made the same point: overseas developments were complicating their already tough task of bringing inflation all the way back to 2.5%, preferably by the end of next year.
Taking the lion’s share of the blame for worsening cost of living pressures may not be completely fair, but it is the price of incumbency – as the latest Essential poll showed.

blocks.caption: Inflation is ‘too high’, but RBA says Australia is not heading for recession – video

blocks.text: Nearly a third of voters believe that government spending is the top cause for rising cost of living.
Only 24% said overseas events like the global oil shock was the main reason, and 19% said it was supermarket price gouging.
While government spending may not be the main reason that inflation has tracked higher since the middle of the year, it is part of the mix.
Economists including Chris Richardson, the country’s top budget watcher, have argued that public spending is too high and is not helping in the battle to bring inflation down.
Government expenditure as a share of the economy is around record highs.

This is hard to reconcile with Chalmers’ protestations that the government has nothing to do with the latest jump in cost of living, particularly when RBA officials frequently refer to the capacity pressures that existed when war on Iran started in late February.
It’s also important to note that the RBA’s preferred measure of underlying inflation – removing the biggest price moves – also lifted from 3.6% to 3.7% in the year to the September quarter.
Regardless of who or what is to blame, and to what degree, voters are likely to get angrier still next Tuesday when the Reserve Bank surely delivers the year’s fifth interest rate hike.

In Senate estimates before the latest price statistics were released, Reserve Bank officials confirmed they were more worried about inflation becoming entrenched than they were about rising unemployment, which recently reached a five-year high.
So it’s hard to see anything but more pain for mortgage holders come Melbourne Cup day. Another rate rise will bring the cash rate to 4.85% – the highest since the GFC.

If you’re starting to fret about that comparison, Sarah Hunter, the RBA’s chief economist, offered the reassurance that there were no signs the economy was “in or heading into a recession in the near term”.
Perhaps, but there is no doubt we are heading into more dangerous territory, and the future is looking darker, not brighter.
Families are approaching Christmas with rates at their highest since 2008, sky-high petrol costs, and rising unemployment.
For many households, it will be a tough summer that will add to an increasingly entrenched pessimism about the future.
The share of Australians saying they think the country is on the wrong track has been steadily climbing and reached 61%, according to the latest Essential poll.
Only 25% of voters think the opposite.
The pressure is now on Chalmers to use December’s mid-year budget to somehow change the narrative as the government approaches the third year of this parliamentary term.
It will be a tough ask, and there are no obvious answers.
There is, at least, one thing we can agree on. As the treasurer is fond of saying: the Middle East conflict can’t end soon enough.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No report of Trump courtesy call on Sara; Marcos remains president
articles.summary: Trump is coming for the ASEAN Summit hosted by Marcos, and Duterte remains Vice President on trial in the Senate

blocks.text: Claim: US President Donald Trump will make a courtesy call on Vice President Sara Duterte when he visits the Philippines next month, and Duterte will be the president by then.
Why we fact-checked this: On October 22, Facebook user Rey Cano Salarda published a post that carries the claim.

It is a text card on a green background that reads, “U.S PRES TRUMP WILL VISIT PHIL. NEXT MONTH COURTESY CALL TO VP SARA, SI VP SARA NA PALA ANG PRESIDENTE NEXT MONTH” (So VP Sara will already be President next month).
As of writing, the post has 29,000 reactions, 2,200 comments, and 1,200 shares.

The facts: There is no report, Palace statement, or White House announcement about a planned Trump courtesy call on Duterte. Trump’s planned visit will be for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, which is hosted by the Philippines.

Also, Duterte will most likely not be replacing Marcos as the president next month. Marcos remains in office, and he has not resigned or been removed. Under Article VII, Section 8 of the Constitution, the Vice President takes over only if the President dies, becomes permanently disabled, is removed, or resigns.
The Palace has dismissed as “delusional” claims from Duterte’s camp that the Vice President is ready to replace Marcos.

Duterte is currently on trial before the Senate impeachment court. The trial resumes on November 9, when her defense team begins presenting its evidence on the remaining unexplained wealth article. The trial may or may not lead to her conviction and removal from office, not elevate her. (READ: Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Sara, who benefits?)

Trump’s visit: Malacañang confirmed on October 14 that Trump will attend the ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that while it is confirmed, the rest of the details will not come from her.

The summits run from November 16 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City. The Philippines chairs ASEAN this year. Marcos declared those days as special non-working days in Metro Manila.

The White House said Trump will take part in the summit on November 16 before heading to Shenzhen, China for the APEC summit. A US official said Marcos has been inviting Trump for some time. This will be his first visit to the Philippines since 2017.

At the summits, Trump will meet ASEAN leaders and other dialogue partners. The Department of Foreign Affairs expects leaders of China, Japan and South Korea to attend, along with UN Secretary-General António Guterres for the ASEAN-UN Summit. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

articles.title: Bato dela Rosa's camp asks SC anew to issue TRO amid P50-M bounty
articles.summary: Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa"s camp has asked the Supreme Court (SC) anew to issue a temporary restraining order (TRO) against his International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant, noting that the…

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 1:50pm

Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa’s camp has asked the Supreme Court (SC) anew to issue a temporary restraining order (TRO) against his International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant, noting that the government has raised a P50-million reward for his arrest.
In a 15-page manifestation, Dela Rosa’s camp also asked the SC to resolve his pending motion for reconsideration on its denial of his prayer for interim relief in May.
“The motion for reconsideration remains unresolved. In the meantime, the enforcement posture it documented has not abated. It has escalated,” it said.

Dela Rosa’s camp noted that the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has dubbed the senator as “armed and dangerous,” placed a P50 million reward for his arrest, declared that the “gloves come off,” and created a task force for his arrest, among others.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla bared the bounty last week, two days after he said Dela Rosa is under the protection of a group in Mindanao, with whom the government is initiating negotiations. He said an operation to get the former Philippine National Police chief could result in 10,000 deaths.
“Significantly, the bounty was announced by DILG Secretary Juanito Victor C. Remulla, who is himself a named Respondent in this case,” Dela Rosa’s camp said.

“A Respondent has thus, while this Honorable Court’s ruling on reconsideration is pending, placed a price on the capture of the very Petitioner whose constitutional challenge he is answering,” it added.
For its part, Malacañang has urged the senator to face his case before the ICC, saying he should not be afraid if his conscience is clear.
Authorities attempted to serve the warrant against Dela Rosa on May 11 while he was in the Senate. He was later placed under protective custody by the upper chamber.
He has not appeared on Senate premises since slipping out on May 14 after “hitching a ride" with Senator Robin Padilla. —AOL, GMA News
